courses.title: Global Politics
courses.description:
(UGEC2352 is double-coded with GLSD2301.)

This course aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to global politics, focusing in particular on its origins and historical evolution, its key concepts, major theoretical frameworks, main actors and institutions, the global architecture of power, and its dynamic nature in the process of globalization. It aims to offer students with the basic knowledge and analytical tools for making sense of current issues in global politics. It adopts a multi-disciplinary approach that integrates theoretical issues with regional case studies.

The course will first offer a general survey of the key concepts and major theoretical perspectives in the study of Global Politics (Liberalism, Realism, Social Constructivism and Marxist theory, etc.). It then proceeds to cover selected topics of global politics in the areas of War and Peace and the Clash of Civilization. It focuses on how world politics is transformed by globalization, with a particular focus on its impacts on issues concerning the identity and national pride, balance of power, peace and conflicts, borders and security, etc. Finally, the course will be concluded with the discussion of latest trends of global governance, with a particular focus on the emergency of international and regional organizations. Relevant real world examples and case studies will be adopted to illustrate the big ideas and key concepts of global politics.

This course intends to promote students’ appreciation of the role of ‘power’, ‘security’ and ‘justice’ in shaping the global political order nowadays. Students will gain deeper insights into not only latest developments in global political affairs, but also concepts and theories useful for further studies in politics, international relations, and global political economy. The course is designed to introduce essential concepts, major theoretical perspectives and basic mechanisms of global political order, allowing students to communicate issues in world politics effectively in group work and individually, in oral as well as written forms.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken UGEC2610/GPAD2345 or UGEC2683/GPAD2355.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

* 1.* *Describe the evolution of the global political order and identify how power relations is related to the peace and security of world politics;*

* 2.* *Understand and apply the basic concepts, theories and analytical approaches of global politics in understanding the interactions between states as well as the dynamics of the competition among great powers;*

* 3.* *Critically analyze the basic characteristics, process and institutions of global political order in* *national, regional and international* *levels;*

* 4.* *Describe and analyze the roles and functions of major international institutions and organizations, such as United Nations, in maintaining global peace and security;*

* 5.* *Analyze the role of the nation-states in the context of the globalized world*

* 6.* *Engage in debates on controversial world issues and reflect critically on different viewpoints**; and*

* 7.* *Develop better cross-cultural and geopolitical awareness necessary for a global citizen.*

If possible, seminar by invited guest will be arranged to provide students with insights into the debates and controversies in contemporary global political order.

courses.required_readings:
* *Teaching Plan and Readings**

The following required readings only serve as the recommended references for this subject and you are encouraged to go to the library to explore other references on your own. Please feel free to consult the instructor as and when necessary. **Readings with asterisk\* are required references** that are most pertinent to part of the final quiz.

Notes:

1. This is a tentative keyword syllabus. We may adjust the pace and coverage based on your progress.

2. Always start with Heywood, and then read the rest as much as you can.

3. For full citations of the publications, please refer to § V above.

* *Part I: A Theoretical Framework in Understanding Global Politics**

* *Lecture 1: Introduction to Global Politics (I)**

Focus: Globalization, Global Politics and the Dynamics of Global Political Order

Key questions

- What do we mean by global politics?

- How does the idea of globalization challenge the inter-states politics?

Suggested readings:

- ***\*******Heywood****, ch.1*

- ***\*******Baylis****, ch.**1 and ch.2*

* *Lecture 2: Introduction to Global Politics (II)**

Focus: The Historical Background of Global Political Order; Globalization, States and Non-State Actors

Suggested readings:

- ***\*******Heywood****, ch.**2, ch.5 and ch.6*

Optional readings:

- *Jack Snyder, “One World, Rival Theories,” Foreign Policy, Nov/Dec 2004, pp.53-62.*

- *Stephen Krasner, “Think Again: Sovereignty,” Foreign Policy, Jan/Feb 2001, pp.20-29.*

- ***Karns****, M. P., Mingst, K. A., & Stiles, K. W. (2015). Nonstate actors: NGOs, Networks, and Social Movements. International organizations: The politics and processes of global governance (pp. 239-277). Boulder, CO: Lynne Rienner.*

* *Lecture 3: Theories of Global Politics (I)**

Focus: Realism versus Liberalism

Key questions

- What makes realist perspectives so popular in the world? How does realism transform itself to fit the contemporary world? Key questions

- Is the global perpetual peace possible? If so, how can we attain global perpetual peace?

Suggested readings:

- ***\*******Heywood****, ch.3*

- ***\*******Baylis****, ch**6, ch.7 and ch.8*

Optional readings:

- ***R&R****, Kenneth Waltz, “The Anarchic Structure of World Politics”, pp.35-56.*

- ***R&R****, David Kang, “Hierarchy and Hegemony in International Politics”, pp.132-135*

- ***R&R****, Hans Morgenthau, “The Future of Diplomacy,” pp.136-145.*

- ***R&R****, Michael Doyle, “Kant, Liberal Legacies, and Foreign Affairs”, pp.111-124.*

- ***Karns****, M. P., Mingst, K. A., & Stiles, K. W. (2015). The theoretical foundations* *of global governance. International organizations: The politics and* *processes of global governance (pp. 43-58). Boulder, CO: Lynne Rienner.*

- *Waltz, Kenneth (1990). “Realist Thought and Neorealist Theory”. Journal of International Affairs. No. 44. Spring/Summer. pp. 21 – 37.*

- *Jervis, Robert (1978). “Cooperation under Security Dilemma”. World Politics. Vol. 30:2. pp. 167 – 214.*

- *Wang, Yuan Kang (2004). “Offensive Realism and the Rise of China”. Issues and Studies. Vol. 40:1. pp. 173 – 201.*

- *Doyle, Michael (1986). “Liberalism and World Politics”. American Political Science Review. Vol. 80:4. pp. 1151 – 1169.*

- *Richardson, James (1997). “Contending Liberalisms: Past and Present”. European Journal of International Relations. Vol. 3:1. pp. 5 – 33.*

- *Andrew Morvasick, “Taking Preference Seriously: A Liberal Theory of International Relations”, International Organization, vol.51, no.4, 1997, pp.513-553.*

* *Lecture 4: Theories of Global Politics (II)**

Focus: Social Constructivism and Marxist Theories

Key questions

- Is the world we lived really “real”? What is the role of identity in international relations? How do the norms and words shape the behaviours of the state?

- What is the relationship between capitalism and the global order? How hegemony is built and is there a way-out?

courses.recommended_readings:
* *(****a) Textbooks:**

* 1.* *Heywood, Andrew (2014) Global Politics, Palgrave **(Heywood)** [Written by the same author of your key text for Introduction to Political Studies, this is an updated text with good coverage – and very easy to read! We will follow this book quite closely.]*

* 2.* *Baylis, John et al. (2014) The Globalization of World Politics: An Introduction to International Relations (6e), Oxford UP **(Baylis)** [Just slightly more advanced than Heywood, this text is comprehensive and clearly written. Each chapter is written by renowned expert(s) on that topic. Highly recommended if you intend to do degree study in IS or global studies.]*

* 3.* *Karns, M. P., Mingst, K. A., & Stiles, K. W. (2015). International organizations: The politics and processes of global governance. Boulder, CO: Lynne Rienner. **(Karns)***

* *(b) More advanced texts**

* *[ALL of these books contain discussion beyond the level expected of this course. For your further study.]**

* 1.* *Beeson, M. and N. Bisley (2013) Issues in Twenty-first Century World Politics, Palgrave **(B&B)** [Succinct and updated chapter-long reviews of key topics in today’s world politics.]*

* 2.* *O’Brien Robert and Marc Williams (2014) Global Political Economy, Palgrave **(GPE)** [A good textbook on the politics of global economics issues; especially useful for our topic on “global governance”]*

* 3.* *Robert Art and Robert Jervis (editors), International Politics: Enduring Concepts and Contemporary Issues, 11th edition, Boston: Prentice Hall, 2013. **(R&R)***

* *(c) Useful references:**

* 1.* *Boyd, Andrew and Joshua Comenetz (2007) An Atlas of World Affairs, Routledge **(Boyd)** [One of the most established and authoritative in the field, this is a concise, accurate and highly readable reference for students of world affairs – especially useful for preparing the map section in the final quiz!]*

* 2.* *Mingst, Karen and Jack Snyder (eds.) (2011) Essential Readings in World Politics (4e), Norton [Good collection of classic articles and excerpts of famous books on world politics.]*

* 3.* *Stiles, Kendall (2011) Case Histories in International Politics, Pearson [Good and readable collection of important cases in IR– a useful source for some presentation topics.]*

courses.title: Analysis of Global Popular Culture
courses.description: Global popular culture includes music, games, movies and videos that cuts across geographical boundaries. This course examines the cultural, social, political and economic implications of global popular culture. The course will introduce to students theories, concepts and tools in the emerging field and encourage students to assess the consumption of global popular culture in their daily life.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken COMM4191
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking this course, students are expected to:

1. Understand the cultural logic of global political economy behind the production and circulation of popular culture.

2. Understand the interplay between the daily consumption of cultural product and the changing socio-political order on local and global levels

courses.title: Sports and World Politics
courses.description: This course examines the relationship between Sports and World politics, in particular about the evolution of global political economy through various sports events like the Olympic Games and World Cup. Taking different sport games as case studies, this course aims to raise attention about some ongoing debates on the global political arena, e.g. Separatism, regional identity, global democracy. It also encourages students to think critically how politics and sports are mutually shaping each other.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After completing this course, students are expected to demonstrate abilities to:
1) Understand the relationship between Global Politics and World Sports
2) Understand sports from a political structure and landscape
3) Analyze various global issues through sports events.

courses.subject: GLSD
courses.title: Korea and the World: Politics, Economy and Culture
courses.description: This course examines the connection between Globalization and South Korea after World War II. It is also interested in accounting for the changes of political, economic, social and cultural aspects of South Korea in the last few decades and the transformation of the attitudes towards Globalization in South Korean society. This course will cover a variety of topics ranging from i) brief overview of the historical development of South Korea since WWII; ii) driving forces and features of the economic developments, iii) their foreign policy concerns, iv) the characteristics of the traditional cultural identities, v) the recent Korean-wave phenomenon; vi) opportunities and challenges brought by Globalization to Korean society.

courses.subject: GLSD
courses.title: Social Innovation and Sustainable Development
courses.description:
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to social innovation as a driver for sustainable development, equipping students to address complex social, economic, and environmental challenges. This course is collaborated with Underwood International College, Yonsei University, featuring both face-to-face sessions led by CUHK teaches and online synchronous class sessions led by Yonsei.

Part I establishes foundational concepts, tracing the history of social innovation and its link to the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including mission-driven business models. Part II explores the three pillars of sustainable development—Social, Economic, and Environmental—examining social innovation in sectors such as sustainable communities, inclusive economies, and green technologies. Part III focuses on practical application, guiding students through developing a social venture—from problem definition to business modeling, impact measurement, and ethical leadership. The course culminates in a group project where students create their own social venture plan.

A unique feature is a field trip to Seoul, South Korea, offering students firsthand exposure to East Asia's dynamic social innovation ecosystem and enriching their final projects with cross-cultural insights.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

* Articulate the core concepts, historical context, and key theories of social innovation and sustainable development.
* Analyze the role of social entrepreneurship in addressing the three pillars of the SDGs (Social, Economic, Environmental).
* Critically evaluate real-world social innovation cases to identify successful strategies and common challenges.
* Apply design thinking and business modeling tools to develop a viable plan for a new social venture with measurable social impact.
* Demonstrate effective teamwork, communication, and presentation skills through collaborative projects and in-class discussions.
* Gain cross-cultural competency through interacting and working with Korean students.
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Introduction: What is social innovation? Social innovation and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)**
The history and theories linking social innovation to sustainable development. The limitations of current development models.

* *The social pillar: Building sustainable communities**
Focusing on SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities). Exploring governance models and socio-ecological transitions.

* *The economic pillar: Inclusive growth and innovation**
Focusing on SDG 1, 8, & 9 (No Poverty, Decent Work, Industry/Innovation). The role of social innovation in the sharing economy and sustainable consumption.

* *The environmental pillar: Green innovation for the planet**
Focusing on SDG 7, 12, & 13 (Affordable/Clean Energy, Responsible Consumption, Climate Action). Examining green technology, renewable energy, and resource efficiency.

* *Defining the challenge and designing the social innovation solution**
How to identify a social problem, analyze stakeholders, and use design thinking to develop a user-centered solution.

courses.subject: GLSD
courses.title: Developmental Study: Poverty, Inequality and Welfare of the World
courses.description: This course aims at providing a critical and theoretical overview of the issues, processes, and responses central to poverty, inequality and welfare around the World. It relates the challenges encountered by these developing states with the dark-sides of the Globalization. This course covers topics including, but not limited to, i) Theoretical understanding of Development and Poverty; ii) Development and Modernization: Asia as examples; iii) Dependency and World Systems Theories: Latin America as examples; iv) Colonization and Cultural Imperialism; iv) Equality in various aspects: Gender, Labour, Food and Wealth; v) International Institutions in ameliorating/aggravating poverty.

courses.subject: GLSD
courses.title: Global Development: Markets, States, Societies and IOs
courses.description: This course aims to provide in-depth analysis of inter-disciplinary global issues using basic principles of economics. This course is built on the introductory economics with respect to the International Political Economy (IPE) framework i.e., the roles of markets, states, society, and International Organizations (IOs) will be elaborated throughout the course. Hence, prior knowledge of introductory economics and the IPE theory are recommended. The course covers growth and human capital theories, and case studies of how policies are developed and implemented to address global issues. Issues discussed in the course include human capital development, economic development and widening inequality, education, social protection, human rights, emergencies and responses including both natural disaster and man-made conflicts, aging population, disadvantaged populations such as disabilities and ethnic minority, energy, and environment.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students deepen understanding of
a. Various global development problems in the contemporary world, and
b. Theories for economic development and human capital development.
2. Policy and practice of global issues are understood through a case-study approach.
3. The roles of markets, states, society and international organizations to address global issues are appreciated.
4. A habit of critical thinking is developed.
5. The skills to apply the knowledge into daily lives are acquired to act as a change maker to address global issues locally.

courses.subject: GLSD
courses.title: New Security Challenges: Terrorism, Ethnic Conflicts and Human Trafficking
courses.description: This course furthers the studies of security challenges to the so-called "Non-Traditional Security" field which becomes more outstanding under Globalization by undermining the role of states in terms of the ability to mobilize force. Unlike another course emphasizing states as the primary actors in Global Security, this course puts more emphasis on how individuals, non-state actors and International Organizations have taken up the responsibilities to uphold the Global Order. This course puts special focus on: i) Terrorism, ii) Ethnic conflicts, and iii) other human security challenges including immigration, energy, health problems.
